summary: This excerpt from Book 4 of a fiction work depicts the climax and aftermath of a city siege. Valentine, Trover and Ana confront a line of soldiers, and a captured wizard is undone when Valentine reveals her hearing aids are recording him. The narrative then skips forward through the days after the wizard's arrest: the sky-cars strike enemy soldiers, the city's printers, robots and lifts are restored, and the siege ends fourteen days later. Valentine and Trover bury their mother in a square grave among hundreds of thousands of dead, each marked HERO OF THE SIEGE.
one_line: In Book 4, Valentine captures a wizard on record and the siege ends two weeks later, with the siblings burying their mother.
key_facts: Ana sees a line of soldiers in the road carrying weapons ranging from knives to old gunpowder weapons to small floppy sidearms.
Ana says "I knew it would be today" and tells Valentine that when she came back that morning, she knew it would be today.
The wizard says "It's all gone" and "You won't get a scrap of it," and adds "We were on your side, you know."
The general replies "You were very well-fed" to the wizard.
Valentine reveals to the wizard that her hearing aids are recording him and asks if he has any words for the microphone.
Three days after the wizard's arrest, the sky-cars lift off again and drop intelligent motes that burrow into enemy soldiers' noses, ears and eyes until their brains are destroyed.
Four days after the wizard's arrest, the printers start to supply food and drugs.
Clever wormy robots inoculate the zombies.
Ten days after the wizard's arrest, the buildings start to repair themselves and the lifts all work again at once.
Fourteen days after the wizard's arrest, the siege ends.
Valentine and Trover bury their mother that morning in the woods, in a perfectly square grave the robots excavated.
Each grave among the hundreds of thousands is marked with a small plaque bearing a name, a date of birth, sometimes a day of death, and the legend HERO OF THE SIEGE.
Trover does not speak all day but tosses in the first shovelful of dirt at their mother's grave.
The survivors wail and tear their clothes while shoveling at the massed dead, and the soldiers laugh.
